title: The arcade, end to end
subtitle: Decision walkthrough · 10 Nov 2026 · narrated by Duo's house voice
posterLine: The whole cabinet experience in five short chapters, then five decisions. Tap play and listen; it stops when it needs you.
footer: Built with the decision-walkthrough skill from docs/design/arcade-ux-walkthrough/spec.json in game-studio-arcade. Answers are saved in this page and sent to director-game-studio-arcade.

lines.text: This is the arcade design, for the cabinet in the basement that makes its own games.
You asked for three things. The whole experience, a screen after each game asking about changes, and a fun but honest limit on making.
It's all drawn on one canvas, fifty-five boards at the cabinet's real size. This walks you through the idea, then asks for five decisions.

chapters.title: The loop the kids live in

lines.text: Here's the loop the kids live in. It starts on the shelf.
They pick Make, say their idea, and answer Claude's questions with the joystick.
A few minutes later the game is ready, and they play it.
When they press escape, the cabinet asks them to check a rule or two, then asks if they want to change anything.
A change makes a new version. Nothing is ever deleted.

chapters.title: What today's live games taught us

lines.text: Two real games were made through these screens today, and they shaped the design.
Each one cost about fifty-five cents and took six to eight minutes.
The plan ran to nineteen rules over six screens, so the new plan fits on one.
Games now open with how to play, a typed idea waits for you to confirm it, and progress only moves forward.
Then the coins. You've already settled most of this.
There's one family pot. A hundred coins, which is ten real dollars, filled on the first of each month.
A make is charged what it really cost, about six coins, and everyone can see who used what.
Spending starts only when a kid presses the coin button.
A make that runs over still finishes. The pot goes negative until the first, and there are no refunds.
Changing games is settled too.
Anyone can change any game. When Alina changes hers, it becomes the next version, and the old one is kept.
When Owen changes it, he gets his own version, and Alina's stays the same.
The change screen shows after every game, starters too, with at most two quick checks first.

chapters.title: How versions show on the shelf
chapters.ask: How should versions show on the shelf?
chapters.why: You asked to see the options first. Same games in all four.

lines.text: First decision. How versions show on the shelf.
All four hold the same games: Alina's penguin game on version three, and Owen's version built on it.
I recommend family rows.

options.label: A. Family rows
options.desc: Newest version one press to play; others' versions indented under it.

lines.text: Family rows. The newest is one press to play, and Owen's version sits under Alina's. Remixes make the shelf longer.

options.label: B. Folders
options.desc: One row per game family; open it to play.

lines.text: Folders. One row per game, and you open it to play. The shortest shelf, one more press.

options.label: C. Big tiles
options.desc: Art first, six a screen, stacked cards for versions.

lines.text: Big tiles. Art first, six games a screen, stacked cards for versions. The names get small.

options.label: D. Flat list
options.desc: Every version its own row, newest first.

lines.text: A flat list, newest first. Simplest, but related games drift apart.

chapters.title: How much of the plan a kid sees
chapters.ask: How much of the plan should a kid see before building?
chapters.why: Today's live plan was 19 rules over 6 screens. The full rules stay one press away in every option.

lines.text: Second. How much of the plan a kid sees before building.
Every option keeps the full rules one press away. I recommend one screen.

options.label: A. One screen
options.desc: The idea, how to play, and the top four rules.

lines.text: One screen. The idea, how to play, and the four rules that matter most, so a kid can spot a wrong one before coins are spent.

options.label: B. Three pages
options.desc: The idea, how to play, what happens; one page each.

lines.text: Three short pages, like a story. Bigger words, but three presses before building.

options.label: C. Just what you'll check
options.desc: The idea, the controls, and the rules you'll be asked about.

lines.text: Just the rules they'll check. The shortest, but the score and the lives stay a surprise.

chapters.title: The real spend limit and overruns
chapters.ask: How should the real account limit work with overruns?
chapters.why: The pot is $10 and the cabinet's workspace limit (D157) is also $10, so an overrun would be cut off.

lines.text: Third, a question your answers raised.
The pot is ten dollars, and the real limit on the cabinet's account is ten dollars too.
So a make that runs over would hit it and stop halfway, which you said shouldn't happen.

options.label: A. Raise the account limit to $13
options.desc: The pot stays 100 coins; any make can finish.

lines.text: I recommend raising the account limit to thirteen dollars. The pot stays a hundred coins, and every make can finish.

options.label: B. Keep $10; no new makes after 94 coins
options.desc: Leaves room for one overrun to finish.

lines.text: Or keep ten dollars, and stop new makes at ninety-four coins, leaving room to finish.

options.label: C. Keep $10 and accept a rare cut-off
options.desc: The kids see the Studio-resting screen.

lines.text: Or keep ten dollars and accept that a rare one gets cut off.

chapters.title: When the pot is too low to start
chapters.ask: When is the pot too low to start a make?
chapters.why: You said the cabinet won't start a make the pot can't cover, but the real cost is only known at the end.

look.label: Canvas · L1 Pot too low for a new game

lines.text: Fourth. When is the pot too low to start?
The cabinet won't start what the pot can't cover, but the real cost is only known at the end.

options.label: A. The usual cost: 6 new, 3 change
options.desc: With 5 coins left, a change can start but a new game can't.

lines.text: I recommend the usual cost. With five coins left, a change can start, but a new game can't.
Or anything above zero. More makes, and more overruns.

options.label: C. The worst case: 30 coins
options.desc: No overruns; the end of the month goes quiet.

lines.text: Or wait for thirty coins, the most a make can cost. No overruns, but the end of each month goes quiet.

chapters.title: Leftover coins on the 1st
chapters.ask: What happens to unused coins when a new month starts?
chapters.why: The canvas assumes the pot fills back to 100, so it always matches $10.

lines.text: Last, an assumption to check. When a month ends with coins left over, what happens?

options.label: A. The pot fills back to 100

lines.text: I drew it filling back to a hundred, so the pot always matches ten real dollars.

options.label: B. Leftovers carry over
options.desc: Saving is rewarded; a month can cost more than $10.

lines.text: Or leftovers carry over, so twelve unused coins make December a hundred and twelve. Saving pays, but a month can cost more than ten dollars.
That's all five. Your answers go to the director, and the canvas gets updated to match.
Every screen is on the canvas if you want to click through it.
